flashcards.q: Define MCAR, MAR, and MNAR with one example each.
flashcards.a: MCAR: missingness independent of everything (a sensor randomly drops readings). MAR: missingness depends on OTHER OBSERVED variables (income missing more for self-employed, and employment type is recorded). MNAR: missingness depends on the MISSING value itself (high earners refuse to report income).

flashcards.q: Can you test whether data is MAR?
flashcards.a: No. You can only test the MCAR null hypothesis (Little's test, 1988, or the practical proxy of checking whether missingness correlates with observed columns). Rejecting MCAR tells you you're in MAR-or-MNAR, but MAR vs MNAR is fundamentally untestable from observed data alone since it hinges on the unobserved values.

flashcards.q: Why is mean imputation dangerous even when data is MCAR?
flashcards.a: It collapses variance -- every imputed value is identical, so imputed rows contribute zero to any variance-based estimate (correlation, feature importance) even though the true missing values would have varied. Under MCAR this just dilutes signal proportionally to missingness rate; under MAR/MNAR it's outright biased on top of that.

flashcards.q: How do XGBoost and LightGBM handle missing values, and where does that break in production?
flashcards.a: At each split they try sending missing values both left and right during training and keep whichever direction minimizes loss -- a learned, per-split default direction, not a fixed fill. It breaks when a feature that was ALWAYS populated in training starts having nulls at inference: the model never learned a direction for it, so it falls back to a fixed default (documented as right branch) that may be arbitrarily wrong.

flashcards.q: What is the single highest-leverage feature engineering move for a MAR/MNAR column that most people skip?
flashcards.a: A binary was_missing indicator column alongside whatever value-fill you use. The fact that a field is missing is frequently more predictive than any value you could impute for it, since missingness is often driven by something meaningful.

flashcards.q: KNNImputer vs IterativeImputer (MICE) -- when do you pick each, and what's the sklearn default n_neighbors for KNNImputer?
flashcards.a: KNNImputer (default n_neighbors=5): simpler, faster, good with local structure, degrades under curse of dimensionality. IterativeImputer/MICE: models each column as a function of all others via a real regression model per column, iterating to convergence (default max_iter=10); better for complex conditional relationships, higher cost, ~O(k*n*p^3*min(n,p)) worst case.

flashcards.q: Does a single IterativeImputer/MICE run give you valid statistical inference?
flashcards.a: No. Valid inference requires MULTIPLE imputation: run the process several times with different random draws, fit the downstream model on each completed dataset, and pool estimates/variances via Rubin's rules. A single sklearn IterativeImputer call gives one point estimate per missing value with no built-in uncertainty quantification.

flashcards.q: You see age with a minimum of -999 and a 25th percentile of 24. What's happening and why won't isna() catch it?
flashcards.a: -999 is an unlabeled sentinel for 'unknown,' not a real age -- disguised missing data, not null. isna() only counts actual NaN/None, not sentinel values sitting as valid-looking numbers. Recode explicitly (replace(-999, np.nan)) then treat it as genuinely missing and diagnose the mechanism.

flashcards.q: What is silent truncation and how does it manifest?
flashcards.a: A field gets cut off at a fixed length (legacy VARCHAR(50), fixed-width export) with no error raised. Manifests as categorical values that should match failing to match across systems (truncated prefix vs full string), inflating category cardinality and breaking joins/encodings.

flashcards.q: Why can't you rely on df.duplicated() alone to catch problematic duplicate rows?
flashcards.a: df.duplicated() only catches exact row equality, which misses near-duplicates from silent truncation, floating-point precision differences, or partial re-ingestion with a slightly different timestamp. Use a true business key (transaction ID, hash of immutable fields) instead.

flashcards.q: What is mojibake and why is it dangerous specifically for ML pipelines?
flashcards.a: Garbled characters from reading a file with the wrong encoding (UTF-8 read as Latin-1: 'café' becomes 'cafÃ©'). It's dangerous because it doesn't throw an error -- it silently inflates categorical cardinality with corrupted duplicates of the same real category, and shreds text features into meaningless byte-garbage tokens.

flashcards.q: When is it acceptable to just drop rows with missing values instead of imputing?
flashcards.a: When missingness is low (rough rule of thumb under ~5%) and verified (not assumed) MCAR -- dropping is simpler and the information loss is negligible. Also standard when the missing field is the label itself, which generally can't be imputed.

flashcards.q: What is the risk of running KNNImputer on data with hundreds of unscaled features?
flashcards.a: It hits the curse of dimensionality the same way distance-based classification does -- 'nearest' neighbors in high-dimensional space stop being meaningfully close -- and unscaled features with larger raw ranges dominate the Euclidean distance calculation, biasing which neighbors get selected regardless of true similarity.
